lead: Finite automata and regular expressions recognise fixed patterns quickly, with no memory of how many times something has happened. A scanner, a form validator, a packet filter and a lift controller all decide from a small fixed set of states. This chapter shows where those machines sit in real software and where the model stops: unbounded counting, nested brackets and backreferences are outside it.
prereq: You need: regular expression operators, Thompson's construction, and decision properties of regular languages.

sections.h3: Scanners turn a character stream into tokens

blocks.text: A compiler, interpreter or JSON reader begins with characters and needs tokens: named pieces such as an identifier, a number, a keyword or an operator. Each token class is a fixed pattern, so each is a regular language. Over letters and digits, an identifier is letter (letter | digit)*, using the operators from chapter 2.1.
The scanner, also called the lexer, is built in five steps.

items: Write one regular expression for each token class: identifier, number, keyword, operator.
Convert each expression to an ε-NFA and merge them into one machine with a single start state, as in chapter 2.3.
Apply subset construction (chapter 2.2) to get one DFA whose accepting states are tagged with the token class they report.
Run the DFA from the current input position and record the last accepting position reached.
Emit the longest match; on a tie, the class listed first wins. Skip whitespace and comments, then repeat.

blocks.text: Longest match matters. On ifx the keyword rule for if matches 2 characters, but the identifier rule matches all 3, so the scanner emits id(ifx). On if( both rules match 2 characters; the tie goes to the keyword, giving kw(if) then the operator (. Generator tools build the DFA from a list of patterns, so a new token means a new pattern, not new code.
The figure shows a small scanner-style DFA of the same kind: the 10-digit mobile-number checker built in the worked example below, with one number accepted and one rejected.

Text search uses the same machine with a different stopping rule. The pattern is a regular expression and the text is read once, left to right. Build the DFA for the pattern and report a match every time the machine sits in an accepting state. One transition per character gives O(n) time for n characters of text; the DFA size depends on the pattern, not the text.

Validation is strict: the whole string must match. The answer is yes only if the machine consumes the whole string and ends in an accepting state; a run that falls into the dead state, or stops early, rejects. A six-digit PIN, a 10-digit mobile number, a date in dd-mm-yyyy form, a vehicle registration number — each is regular and each is checked in one pass.

A network card, a firewall or a TCP implementation looks for short fixed patterns: a start-of-frame byte, a flag combination, the word GET at the start of an HTTP request line, a closing tag. Such patterns are regular, and a machine can emit a signal on the transition that completes the pattern. In hardware a handful of flip-flops does the job at line rate.

A vending machine that releases a snack after ₹20 is inserted, a traffic light cycling through fixed phases, a lift that opens its door in the stopped state — each has a small fixed set of situations and a fixed response for each. That is a finite automaton with output; Moore and Mealy machines are covered in chapter 2.4.

Every finite automaton has a fixed number of states, so it carries a fixed amount of memory. That memory can hold a counter up to a fixed bound: between 0 and 5 a's is regular, written a{0,5}. It cannot hold a counter that grows with the input. The language {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} needs the machine to remember how many a's it saw and compare that with the number of b's, and no finite state set does that. The pumping lemma (chapter 2.6) makes the argument precise.

Nested structure fails for the same reason. Balanced brackets of arbitrary depth, an arithmetic expression with parentheses inside parentheses, a document with tags inside tags: each needs a stack, so each needs a pushdown automaton or a context-free grammar. A DFA can check the first few levels with one state per depth, but the depth is then capped.

Backreferences are the third limit. The pattern (ab)\1 matches abab by remembering what the group matched and comparing later; that memory is a copy of part of the input, of unbounded length. Engines also offer lookahead, lookbehind and recursive patterns: useful, but outside the mathematical definition. A mathematical regular expression uses only ∅, ε, alphabet symbols, union, concatenation and star, and Kleene's theorem (chapter 2.5) is about exactly that class.

The split has a practical edge. A DFA matcher reads each character once and cannot blow up; a backtracking engine with backreferences can take exponential time on some patterns. Where worst-case speed matters, tools use the finite-automaton core.

spec.aria: A chain of states q0 to q10, the first edge labelled 6–9 and the rest braced as any digit 0–9, with q0 dropping to a dead state d on 0–5, and the two test numbers below.

examples.question: A website form accepts a 10-digit Indian mobile number whose first digit is 6, 7, 8 or 9. (a) Write a regular expression. (b) Give the DFA and count its states. (c) Test 9876543210 and 1234567890.
steps: Alphabet Σ = {0,1,...,9}. The first digit must be in {6,7,8,9}, written [6-9].
The remaining 9 digits are any digit, written [0-9]{9}.
q0 is the start. On 6–9 it moves to q1; on 0–5 it moves to a dead state d, which loops on every digit.
For 1 ≤ k ≤ 9, qk moves to q(k+1) on any digit 0–9; q10 is the only accepting state.
State count: q0 through q10 is 11 states. One extra dead state catches a first digit in 0–5; all later digits are accepted, so 12 states in total.
9876543210: length 10, first digit 9 in {6,7,8,9}; the run ends in q10, so accepted.
1234567890: length 10 but first digit 1 is not in {6,7,8,9}; the run is q0 → d and stays in d. Rejected.
examples.answer: R = [6-9][0-9]{9}; 11 live states plus one dead state, so 12; 9876543210 accepted, 1234567890 rejected.
examples.check:
for n in ["9876543210", "1234567890"]:
    print(len(n))
    print(int(n[0]))
    print(1 if n[0] in "6789" else 0)

examples.question: Use the same DFA on 6789012345 and 987654321 (nine digits).
steps: Pattern [6-9][0-9]{9}. 6789012345: length 10, first digit 6 in {6,7,8,9}; the run reaches q10, so accepted.
987654321: length 9; after the last character the machine sits in q9, which is not accepting. Rejected.
A correct first digit alone is not enough; the length must be exactly 10.
examples.answer: 6789012345 is accepted; 987654321 is rejected because it has only 9 digits.

traps: Treating regex-engine extras as regular. Backreferences, lookahead, lookbehind and recursive patterns are outside Kleene's regular expressions; an examiner will ask for a proof.
Confusing bounded and unbounded counts. a{0,100} is regular because the bound is fixed; aⁿbⁿ is not.
Ignoring longest match: ifx is one identifier id(ifx), not kw(if) plus id(x).
Thinking a DFA needs one state per input character. States count pattern positions: the mobile-number DFA has 12 states whatever the length.
Writing a regular expression for balanced brackets or aⁿbⁿ; those need a stack, so they are not regular.

quiz.q: What is lexical analysis, in one line?
quiz.a: The phase of a compiler or interpreter that groups input characters into tokens such as identifiers, numbers, keywords and operators, using a regular pattern for each token class.

quiz.q: Why does a scanner emit the longest match, and how are ties broken?
quiz.a: Longest match keeps the token as large as possible: ifx becomes one identifier, not keyword if plus identifier x. Ties go to the class listed first, so keywords are listed before identifiers.

quiz.q: Write a regular expression for a 6-digit PIN with no leading zero, and test 012345 and 123456.
quiz.a: Pattern [1-9][0-9]{5}. 012345 starts with 0, not in [1-9], so it enters the dead state and rejects. 123456 has length 6, first digit 1 in [1-9] and five more digits, so it ends accepting.

quiz.q: How many states does a DFA need for [6-9][0-9]{9}, counting the dead state?
quiz.a: States q0 to q10 trace the digits read so far, with q10 accepting: 11 states. One extra dead state catches a first digit in 0–5; all later digits are accepted, so 12 states in total.

quiz.q: Explain why no DFA can decide whether the parentheses in an expression are balanced.
quiz.a: The machine must remember how many brackets are open, and that number can grow without bound. A finite automaton has a fixed number of states, so its memory is fixed. Balanced brackets are therefore not regular, which the pumping lemma confirms; a stack, that is a pushdown automaton, is needed.

quiz.q: A colleague says: Python's re module matches aⁿbⁿ using backreferences, so regular expressions can count. What is wrong with the claim?
quiz.a: The premise is wrong: plain backreferences in Python's re cannot match aⁿbⁿ for arbitrary n. A backreference matches a repeated copy of a captured substring, so (ab)\1 gives abab and (.*)\1 gives {ww}; that says nothing about counting a's against b's. Matching aⁿbⁿ needs recursion (PCRE) or balancing groups (.NET). Even then the conclusion fails: those features store a copy of part of the input, so the memory is unbounded, and such patterns are not regular expressions in the sense of Kleene's theorem.

quiz.q: In a machine with output, what does a Moore machine's output depend on?
quiz.a: Only the current state. A Mealy machine's output depends on the current state and the current input symbol.

quiz.q: Why is a DFA-based text search O(n) in the length of the text?
quiz.a: The machine reads each character exactly once and takes one transition per character, never moving backwards. With n characters there are n transitions, so the time is proportional to n; the DFA size depends only on the pattern.

beyond: Not for the exam. The finite-automaton core is what real string libraries fall back on when worst-case speed matters: linear-time matchers avoid the exponential blow-up of backtracking engines. Speech tools use finite-state transducers, machines that read a symbol and write another on the same transition. Network intrusion detectors compile thousands of byte patterns into one large DFA so a packet is checked in a single pass. Hardware designers draw the same diagrams for bus protocol checkers. Search terms: lexer generator, linear-time regular expression matching, finite-state transducer, DFA-based packet classification.
